content: The longest documented human lifespan belongs to Jeanne Calment of France, who lived from 1875 to 1997, reaching the age of 122 years. At the age of 14, she met the famous artist Vincent van Gogh, an event that later brought her media attention in 1988 when she was 113 years old. Her life has been meticulously documented in the records of her hometown, Arles, leaving no reasonable doubt about her age. The evidence supporting her case is more robust than for any other supercentenarian, making her the gold standard among verified longevity cases. In contrast, the claim of Shigechiyo Izumi of Japan, who was said to have lived to 120 years, has been disputed. Although Guinness World Records still recognizes his age, Japanese authorities have expressed uncertainty about its accuracy. This claim, accepted in 1978, was later questioned as early as 1984, with research suggesting that his birth date might have been confused with that of a younger brother who died in infancy. As of August 13, 2007, following the death of Yone Minagawa, the oldest living person is Edna Parker of the United States, who was born on April 20, 1893, and is currently 114 years old. Alongside her, Maria de Jesus and Bertha Fry are the only other validated individuals born in 1893 who are still alive. Since 1955, when Guinness World Records began tracking such data, a list has been maintained of individuals who have held the title of the world's oldest recognized person. This list is retroactive, meaning some cases, such as Betsy Baker's, were verified only decades later. The record for the longest consecutive time holding the title of World's Oldest Person belongs to Shigechiyo Izumi, who held it for 3,384 days from November 16, 1976, to February 21, 1986. Conversely, the shortest time was held by Emma Tillman of the United States, who held the title for just four days, from January 24 to January 28, 2007. On average, the 36 individuals following Betsy Baker (excluding the current titleholder, Edna Parker) held the title for approximately 525.5 days. The United States has the highest number of individuals on this list, with 12, followed by the United Kingdom with 9 and Japan with 6. The category of oldest living man has been maintained intermittently by Guinness World Records, becoming a permanent category only in 2000. For individuals listed before 2000, the data is based on historical reconstructions. Shigechiyo Izumi also holds the record for the longest consecutive time as the World's Oldest Man, holding the title for 4,367 days from March 9, 1974, to February 21, 1986. The shortest time was held by Henri Pérignon of France, who held the title for just eight days, from June 10 to June 18, 1990. The United States leads in this category as well, with nine individuals, followed by Japan with four and the United Kingdom with three. The field of gerontology, which studies aging and longevity, focuses on tracking the longest-lived individuals as markers of the human lifespan. The discipline is often attributed to Michel Eugène Chevreul, a French chemist who lived to the age of 102, passing away in 1889. Advances in record-keeping, particularly in industrialized nations since the late 19th century, have significantly improved the ability to verify claims of extreme longevity. Modern verification standards require multiple independent documents confirming a birth date, rather than relying solely on the claimant's evidence. Guinness World Records is considered the authority in this field, and claims that fail to meet their standards are categorized as unverified. The lifespans of the world's oldest individuals have been increasing due to advancements in healthcare, improved living conditions, and better record-keeping. These factors, combined with a growing global population, have led to a rise in the number of verified supercentenarians—individuals who live to 110 years or more. In 1837, the oldest verified person was 108 years old, but today it is not uncommon for individuals, particularly women, to surpass 110 years. This emerging demographic has led to the coining of the term supercentenarian to describe these exceptionally long-lived individuals.
